headline: Federal judge blocks Connecticut convertible-pistol ban before it can take effect
dek: A preliminary injunction pauses Connecticut’s new sales and import ban while Glock and industry plaintiffs challenge the law under the Second Amendment.
body: A federal judge has temporarily blocked Connecticut from enforcing a new law that would prohibit the sale, importation and distribution of certain semiautomatic pistols that can be converted into fully automatic weapons. The preliminary injunction came Sept. 30, hours before Public Act 26-41 was scheduled to take effect, and leaves the law in place while the constitutional challenge moves forward. The [U.S. District Court order](https://ecf.ctd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2026cv1528-44=) covers two related cases brought by Glock Inc. and a group that includes the National Shooting Sports Foundation, Shadow Systems and Blue Trail Range Corporation.

Judge Kari A. Dooley did not strike down the statute or decide every question raised by the plaintiffs. Instead, she found for purposes of the preliminary-injunction request that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their Second Amendment claim, were likely to suffer irreparable harm without immediate relief, and had satisfied the other requirements for an injunction. The order says the court is preserving the status quo until the issues can be developed and adjudicated more fully.

The law, House Bill 5043 during the legislative process, defines a convertible pistol as a semiautomatic pistol with a cruciform trigger bar that can be changed by hand or with a common household tool through the attachment of a pistol converter. The law’s definition excludes some hammer-fired pistols and some designs with a shielded trigger bar. For covered pistols manufactured on or after Oct. 1, a person or business that distributes, transports, imports, keeps for sale or offers one for sale would face a Class D felony under the statute. Connecticut’s [official description of the law](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/06-2026/governor-lamont-signs-legislation-prohibiting-the-sale-of-pistols-that-can-easily-be-converted) says the measure targets firearms that can be altered with illegal conversion devices; it does not legalize those devices or converted machine guns.

The dispute turned on how the Second Amendment’s historical test applies to a law aimed at a firearm that is legal in its ordinary, unmodified form. The defendants pointed to founding-era “proving laws” from Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Massachusetts that required firearm inspections or manufacturing standards before sale, along with the longstanding regulation of machine guns. The plaintiffs argued that the historical tradition addresses illegal modifications and converted weapons rather than banning a common semiautomatic handgun because someone might later misuse it.

Dooley wrote that the state’s proposed historical comparisons did not adequately rebut the presumption that the law was unconstitutional at this early stage. The order distinguishes safety inspections before a firearm enters commerce from efforts to prevent future misuse after a firearm has been sold. It also notes that the parties did not dispute that unconverted handguns with cruciform trigger bars are safe and popular for self-defense. The judge cautioned that the result could change after a fuller record is developed.

The ruling has immediate practical consequences for Connecticut gun dealers and manufacturers. The court cited evidence that Blue Trail Range had about $25,000 worth of affected handguns and had stopped ordering new inventory because of the law. The plaintiffs also argued that the statute could disrupt contracts, advertising and sales to law-enforcement customers who were not exempted. Those business and customer claims helped support the court’s finding of irreparable harm, but they remain part of an ongoing lawsuit rather than a final judgment on the statute’s validity.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong has said the state will defend the law, calling its gun-safety provisions lawful and lifesaving. [Connecticut Public](https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-10-02/judge-pauses-ct-ban-on-the-sale-of-guns-that-can-be-turned-into-quick-firing-weapons) reported that the injunction blocks the law from taking effect while the case proceeds. The next phase will determine whether the state can produce a stronger constitutional justification, whether the plaintiffs’ claims survive further litigation and whether the injunction remains in place. Until a later court order changes the situation, the sales ban is paused; the separate prohibition on conversion devices and converted machine guns remains in force.
